title: Second judge blocks Trump's birthright citizenship order, leaving administration facing two injunctions
summary: US District Judge Christopher Cooper in Washington, DC, issued a preliminary injunction on November 25 barring federal agencies from enforcing President Donald Trump's August executive order narrowing birthright citizenship, the second court to block the policy after a Maryland judge ruled in September.
content:
A second federal judge has blocked President Donald Trump's latest attempt to curtail birthright citizenship, dealing another setback to a flagship policy of his administration's hardline immigration crackdown. US District Judge Christopher Cooper in Washington, DC, issued a preliminary injunction on Wednesday, November 25, barring federal agencies from enforcing the president's August executive order against children covered by a class action lawsuit.

The ruling means the Trump administration must now overturn two separate court orders before it can enforce the policy at all. A federal judge in Maryland blocked the same order in September, and the two injunctions together leave the administration with no path to implementation unless both are reversed on appeal, according to [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/trumps-newest-order-curtailing-birthright-citizenship-is-blocked-by-second-judge-2026-11-25/).

Cooper's injunction bars the US Department of State, the Department of Homeland Security and the Social Security Administration from enforcing the order against any children covered by the class action. In practical terms, that means the government cannot refuse passports or Social Security numbers to the children at the centre of the case while the litigation continues.

"The merits in this case are clear-cut," Cooper wrote in a 67-page opinion. "The Supreme Court has twice confirmed that all children born in this country are US citizens, save only for the small handful who are not subject to US law." He added that the Supreme Court had already made clear that "the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws."

The case turns on the citizenship clause of the 14th Amendment to the US Constitution, which confers citizenship on people born in the United States who are "subject to the jurisdiction thereof." In 1898, the Supreme Court ruled in United States v. Wong Kim Ark that the clause guarantees citizenship regardless of the immigration status of a baby's parents. Cooper said the high court's ruling in June of this year embraced that 1898 decision and left no room for the president to narrow it by executive order.

Trump's August order was his second attempt to restrict birthright citizenship. His first order, signed on the first day of his second term in January 2025, sought to deny automatic citizenship to children born in the United States whose parents were neither US citizens nor lawful permanent residents, known as green card holders. In June, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that the initial order violated the 14th Amendment.

Undeterred, the president signed a new, more narrowly drawn order in August. It took aim at so-called "birth tourism," in which women travel to the United States to give birth so their children obtain automatic citizenship. It also targeted children whose parents work for foreign governments or international organisations but lack diplomatic immunity, and children with a parent classified as an "alien enemy."

Cooper found that the new order suffered from the same constitutional defect as the old one. The categories it created, he concluded, were precisely the kind of exceptions the Supreme Court had already said the president cannot invent.

The American Civil Liberties Union, which represented the plaintiffs in the class action, welcomed the ruling. Cody Wofsy, a lawyer at the organisation, said in a statement that Trump "needs to accept that birthright citizenship is the law of the land." "Enough is enough," he said. "The Supreme Court has twice rejected efforts to gut birthright citizenship, in 1898 and again earlier this year. Third time is not the charm."

The White House attacked the decision. Spokeswoman Lauren Bis called it "just another ruling from an activist judge appointed by (former President Barack) Obama attempting to thwart President Trump's commonsense agenda." She said Trump's order was "consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court," signalling that the administration intends to appeal.

The administration's next step is likely an appeal to the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, while the Maryland case proceeds separately toward the Fourth Circuit. Unless the administration wins in both courts, the August order cannot take effect. Legal experts note that the Supreme Court, having already ruled against the first version of the policy in June, would be the likely final arbiter if either appeal reaches it.

For the families at the heart of the case, the ruling preserves the status quo: children born in the United States remain US citizens, entitled to the documents that prove it. But the dispute is far from settled. The administration has shown it is willing to return to the same question with a new order after each defeat, and the courts have now answered twice. Whether a third attempt follows, and how the appeals courts treat the two injunctions, will decide whether birthright citizenship — a right the United States has recognised for more than a century — faces another test in the Supreme Court.

The ruling also fits a wider pattern of the second Trump administration testing the limits of executive power through orders that courts have repeatedly narrowed or blocked. Just this month, the president [signed the Epstein Files Transparency Act into law](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/trump-signs-epstein-files-transparency-act-november-2026) after Congress forced his hand, and [vowed to work with Democrats on capping credit card interest rates at 10 percent](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/trump-vows-work-democrats-cap-credit-card-rates-10-percent-november-2026) — a reminder that the administration's agenda is being shaped as much in the courts and in Congress as in the Oval Office.
